stem: According to the text, why did Calloway conclude that the Wyoming site was once warmer than it is today?
stimulus: Fossilized leaves can record ancient climates as well as ancient plants. For example, paleobotanist Ines Calloway examined leaves of an extinct laurel relative preserved in shale at a site in Wyoming whose rock layers span roughly 50 to 56 million years. In present-day forests, leaves with smooth edges are more common in warm regions, while leaves with toothed edges are more common in cool ones. Because nearly 70 percent of Calloway's specimens had smooth edges, she concluded that the area was once considerably warmer than it is now.
choices: Most of the leaf specimens she examined had smooth rather than toothed edges.
The leaf specimens came from rock layers between 50 and 56 million years old.
The laurel relative she studied is found only in warm regions of the world today.
Leaves with toothed edges are more common than smooth leaves in warm regions today.
explanation: The question asks why Calloway reached her conclusion, so you need the sentence that begins 'Because.' It says nearly 70 percent of her specimens had smooth edges. Put that together with the earlier sentence saying smooth edges are more common in warm regions, and you have her reason. Choice A paraphrases it.

B.why: You picked up the age range, which does appear in the passage. But it tells you when the leaves formed, not why Calloway thought the climate was warmer. It answers a different question.

C.why: The passage says the laurel relative is extinct and never says where it grows. You filled in a reason the text doesn't give. Look for the line that proves the answer before you choose it.

D.why: This reverses the passage. The text says smooth leaves are more common in warm regions and toothed leaves in cool ones. You probably remembered the words but swapped which goes with which.

stem: According to the text, what did Faure's study of merchants' ledgers reveal?
stimulus: Historians have usually attributed the growth of patterned silk weaving in one town in southern France to a mechanical loom installed there in 1782. However, a study of merchants' ledgers by textile historian Odile Faure complicates that account. The ledgers show that the town's output of patterned cloth had already tripled between 1768 and 1776. During those same years, a local dyers' workshop began producing colorfast threads in shades that weavers had previously been forced to import.
choices: The town's output of patterned cloth rose sharply before the mechanical loom arrived.
The mechanical loom tripled the town's output of patterned cloth after 1782.
Weavers stopped importing colored threads once the mechanical loom was installed.
The dyers' workshop was the only cause of the rise in patterned cloth output.
explanation: The ledgers show that output tripled between 1768 and 1776, which is years before the loom was installed in 1782. That is what Faure's study adds after 'However,' and Choice A restates it.

B.why: This is the older view that the 'However' sentence corrects. The tripling took place between 1768 and 1776, before the loom existed, so you gave the loom credit for growth that came earlier.

C.why: The passage connects the end of imported threads to the dyers' workshop in the 1768–1776 period, not to the loom. You attached a real detail to the wrong cause and the wrong date.

D.why: The passage says the workshop's threads appeared during the same years output grew. It never says the workshop was the only cause. 'Only' claims more than the ledgers show.

stem: According to the text, why does Adjei caution against applying the trial's results broadly?
stimulus: Fermented foods such as kefir and miso are often promoted as aids to digestion. In an eight-week trial led by nutritionist Kwame Adjei, 48 adults who added one serving of kefir per day reported less bloating than did a comparison group. Adjei considers it likely that the kefir's live cultures contributed to the effect. He cautions, however, that every participant was already in good health, so the results may not extend to people with chronic digestive disorders, who are the most likely to try such remedies.
choices: The trial's participants did not have chronic digestive disorders.
The trial lasted only eight weeks rather than several months.
The comparison group also reported a decrease in bloating.
The kefir's live cultures probably did not cause the effect.
explanation: The sentence that starts 'He cautions' gives the reason: every participant was already healthy, so the results may not apply to people with chronic digestive disorders. Choice A paraphrases that.

B.why: The passage does mention eight weeks, but Adjei never gives the length of the trial as his concern. You took a number from a different part of the passage that doesn't answer 'why.'

C.why: The kefir group reported less bloating than the comparison group. Nothing says the comparison group improved too, and the passage points the other way.

D.why: Adjei considers it likely that the live cultures did contribute. This reverses his view. His caution is about who was studied, not about what caused the effect.

stem: According to the text, how did Lindqvist's approach differ from that of other engineers of her time?
stimulus: Early twentieth-century engineers who built concrete bridges in mountainous regions typically poured each deck as a single continuous slab and relied on thick steel reinforcement to keep it from cracking. When engineer Marta Lindqvist designed a footbridge across a Norwegian gorge in 1931, she took a different approach. She cast the deck in short segments joined by flexible seams, allowing the concrete to expand and contract with the gorge's sharp temperature swings. Inspectors who examined the bridge in 2019, nearly ninety years later, found almost no cracking.
choices: She built the deck from separate segments instead of one continuous slab.
She used thick steel reinforcement to keep the concrete deck from cracking.
She designed bridges that crossed mountain gorges rather than wide rivers.
She had her bridge inspected for cracks nearly ninety years after building it.
explanation: The first sentence says other engineers poured each deck as a single continuous slab. Lindqvist cast hers in short segments joined by flexible seams. That contrast is the difference, and Choice A states it.

B.why: Thick steel reinforcement was what the other engineers relied on. You gave Lindqvist the method she moved away from.

C.why: The passage says the other engineers also worked in mountainous regions and never mentions rivers. Nothing in the text supports this difference.

D.why: The 2019 inspection is in the passage, but it was done by inspectors, not by Lindqvist, and it shows how her bridge held up rather than how her method differed. You picked a real detail that answers another question.

stem: According to the text, what did Natarajan find when she excavated the seed samples?
stimulus: Farmers have long assumed that weed seeds buried by plowing lose their ability to sprout within a few years. Agronomist Priya Natarajan tested that assumption on plots in Iowa where velvetleaf seeds had been buried at depths of 5 to 20 centimeters. When she excavated samples in 2024, two decades after burial, about 12 percent of the seeds germinated. The finding suggests that plowing may delay, rather than eliminate, a field's weed problem.
choices: Some of the seeds could still sprout twenty years after they were buried.
The seeds had lost their ability to sprout within a few years of burial.
Seeds buried at 20 centimeters sprouted more often than shallower seeds.
Plowing had completely eliminated velvetleaf from the plots she studied.
explanation: The excavation sentence says that two decades after burial, about 12 percent of the seeds germinated. 'Two decades' means twenty years, and 12 percent means some of the seeds. Choice A says exactly that.

B.why: This is the farmers' assumption, which Natarajan's study tested and disproved. You picked the view that the passage sets up only to correct it.

C.why: The 5 to 20 centimeter range describes where the seeds were buried. The passage never compares germination at different depths. You took the edge of a range and attached a finding to it.

D.why: The last sentence says plowing may delay the weed problem rather than eliminate it, and some seeds still sprouted. This choice reverses the conclusion.

stem: According to the text, what leads Vrána to conclude that the hymnbook was made in 1818 or later?
stimulus: Musicologists long assumed that a hymnbook recovered from a Moravian church attic in 1974 dated from the 1790s, when the congregation was founded. However, Ilse Vrána found that its paper carries watermarks from a mill that operated only between 1812 and 1825. She also noticed that several of its melodies use a notation for ornaments that the congregation's organist introduced in 1818, so she concludes that the book could not have been made before that year.
choices: Its paper bears watermarks from a mill that opened in 1812.
The congregation that used it was founded in the 1790s.
It was recovered from a church attic in the year 1974.
Some melodies use a notation the organist adopted in 1818.
explanation: The question asks why Vrána puts the date at 1818 or later. Find the sentence that gives 1818: several melodies use an ornament notation the organist introduced that year, "so she concludes" the book can't be older. Choice D says the same thing in different words.

A.why: You picked up a different piece of dating evidence. The watermarks only show the paper was made between 1812 and 1825, so they can't explain why the book is no earlier than 1818. Every word of this choice is in the passage, but it answers a different question.

B.why: This is the old view that Vrána's evidence overturns. A founding in the 1790s would point to an earlier date, so it can't be her reason for dating the book to 1818 or later.

C.why: 1974 is when the book was found, not evidence of when it was made. You grabbed a date from the first sentence instead of going back to the sentence about 1818.

stem: According to the text, about how long ago does Haddad estimate the granary was destroyed?
stimulus: At Tell Hamra, archaeologists found charred barley beneath a collapsed granary. The pottery in the layer above the barley suggests that the granary is between 3,100 and 3,400 years old. Radiocarbon tests on the barley itself, however, gave an age of about 3,250 years. Because the barley was harvested shortly before the fire, archaeologist Samir Haddad treats that figure as the best estimate of when the granary was destroyed. A smaller storehouse nearby burned about 3,000 years ago.
choices: About 3,400 years ago
About 3,250 years ago
About 3,100 years ago
About 3,000 years ago
explanation: Find the sentence about Haddad. He treats "that figure," the radiocarbon age of about 3,250 years, as the best estimate of when the granary was destroyed. The word "however" tells you this result, not the pottery range, is the one the passage relies on.

A.why: 3,400 is the older end of the pottery range, not Haddad's estimate. You took one edge of a range when the question asked for a single figure.

C.why: 3,100 is the younger end of the pottery range. The passage gives it as the rough first estimate, and the radiocarbon result then narrows it.

D.why: 3,000 years is when a different building, the nearby storehouse, burned. You gave the granary a date that belongs to the storehouse.

stem: According to the text, why were the engineers concerned about the Harlow Street Bridge?
stimulus: Engineers who inspected the Harlow Street Bridge in 2023 found its steel cables in good condition. What concerned them instead were the concrete deck joints, which had cracked after decades of winter road salt seeped through them. The city has proposed replacing the joints with sealed rubber ones, a repair expected to close the bridge for eight months. Commuters, for their part, worry mainly about the long detour the closure will require.
choices: Salt had seeped through the deck joints and cracked them.
The steel cables showed early signs of corrosion.
Replacing the joints would close the bridge for months.
The closure would force drivers onto a lengthy detour.
explanation: The question asks what concerned the engineers. The second sentence answers it directly: the deck joints had cracked after years of road salt seeping through. Choice A says the same thing in different words.

B.why: The passage says the cables were in good condition. This choice reverses what the engineers found.

C.why: The eight-month closure comes from the proposed repair, not from what worried the engineers. You gave the fix as the cause.

D.why: The detour is the commuters' worry, not the engineers'. The detail is in the passage, but it belongs to a different group.

stem: According to the text, what surprised researchers about the March storm?
stimulus: Forecasters expected a March storm crossing the Gulf of Lion to weaken once it reached land, as such storms typically do. At first it behaved as predicted: it lost strength over the coastal plain, and its rainfall there came close to the forecast 40 millimeters. What surprised researchers at the regional weather service was what happened next. Over the foothills, the storm's winds strengthened again, briefly exceeding 90 kilometers per hour.
choices: It lost strength after moving over the coastal plain.
Its rainfall on the coast came close to 40 millimeters.
Its winds grew stronger again once it reached the foothills.
Its rainfall on the coast was far heavier than predicted.
explanation: Find the word "surprised." The passage says what surprised researchers was "what happened next": over the foothills, the winds strengthened again. Choice C says the same thing in different words.

A.why: The storm weakening over the coast is what forecasters expected, so it can't be the surprise. You used a true detail from the passage that answers a different question.

B.why: The 40 millimeters of rain matched the forecast. The passage lists it as part of the expected behavior, not as the surprise.

D.why: The passage says coastal rainfall came close to the forecast. It wasn't far heavier, so this choice reverses the text.

stem: According to the text, how did one runner differ from the others in Mori's study?
stimulus: In a study of twelve elite distance runners, physiologist Aiko Mori measured how each athlete's stride changed over the final kilometer of a 10,000-meter race. Most runners shortened their strides as they tired while keeping their step rate roughly constant. One runner, however, kept nearly the same stride length throughout and instead increased her step rate in the last 400 meters. Mori suggests that this pattern may reduce strain on the hamstrings.
choices: She shortened her strides while holding her step rate steady.
She kept her stride length and quickened her steps near the end.
She kept her step rate constant during the final kilometer.
She suffered less hamstring strain than the other eleven runners.
explanation: The word "however" introduces the runner who was different. She kept nearly the same stride length and increased her step rate in the last 400 meters. Choice B says the same thing in different words.

A.why: This describes what most runners did, not the one who stood out. You took the other runners' behavior and gave it to her.

C.why: A constant step rate was the other runners' pattern. The passage says this runner increased her step rate near the end, so this choice reverses what she did.

D.why: Mori only suggests her pattern "may" reduce hamstring strain, and the study never measured strain. This choice states a guess as a measured result.

stem: According to the text, which statement about the village's fluent whistlers is true?
stimulus: Researchers often credit steep terrain for the survival of whistled speech, since a whistle carries across a valley farther than a shout. When linguist Inés Calderón surveyed a highland village where a whistled form of the local language is still used, she found that explanation incomplete. Residents aged 20 to 35 whistled fluently, while those over 60 rarely did. However, the younger speakers had learned it not from their parents but from a school program begun in 2004, which Calderón concluded now sustains the practice.
choices: Most were over 60 and had learned to whistle at home.
Most had learned to whistle in school, not from their parents.
Most whistled chiefly to call to neighbours across the valley.
Most had founded the village's school program in 2004.
explanation: The question asks what is true of the fluent whistlers, so find the sentence about them. The passage names them as residents aged 20 to 35. The 'However' sentence then says these younger speakers learned it 'not from their parents but from a school program.' Choice B restates that line.

A.why: You took the age group from the wrong sentence. The text says people over 60 rarely whistled. It also says the fluent speakers did not learn it at home.

C.why: You answered with the terrain explanation from the first sentence. That is the view Calderón found incomplete. Nothing in the text says how the fluent whistlers actually use whistled speech.

D.why: The date 2004 is in the passage, but it marks when the school program began. The text never says the whistlers founded it. They were taught by it.

stem: According to the text, when did the fault near Varrel last produce a major earthquake?
stimulus: Small earthquakes can reveal faults that larger ones have not yet exposed. For example, a network of 40 seismometers near the town of Varrel recorded more than 1,200 tremors between 2015 and 2021, none above magnitude 2. Plotted together, their epicentres traced a straight line 14 kilometres long, marking a previously unknown fault. Using layered sediment near that line, the team estimates that the fault last produced a major quake between 600 and 900 years ago.
choices: Sometime between 2015 and 2021
Between 600 and 900 years ago
Precisely 900 years ago
Roughly 1,200 years ago
explanation: Find the sentence that answers 'when' for a major quake. It is the last one: the team estimates the fault's last major quake happened 'between 600 and 900 years ago.' Choice B gives that range exactly as the text states it.

A.why: Those years are when the seismometers recorded the small tremors. The text says none of those tremors was above magnitude 2, so none was a major quake.

C.why: 900 is only the upper end of an estimated range. You treated the edge of an estimate as an exact date, which the text never gives.

D.why: 1,200 is how many tremors the network recorded, not an age in years. That number answers a different question.

stem: According to the text, how did the highest hourly earners differ from other couriers?
stimulus: Economists studying delivery couriers who use a smartphone platform expected those who worked the most hours to earn the most per hour, since experience should make them faster. Over eighteen months, economist Rui Matos tracked the earnings of 310 couriers in one city. However, the highest hourly earners were not the longest-working couriers but those who logged on mainly during the evening rush, when the platform pays a bonus per order. Matos suggests platforms could narrow this gap by spreading bonuses across the day.
choices: They worked more total hours than the other couriers did.
They completed orders faster because of greater experience.
They worked chiefly during hours when orders paid a bonus.
They received bonuses spread evenly across the whole day.
explanation: The 'However' sentence holds Matos's finding. It says the top hourly earners were the couriers who 'logged on mainly during the evening rush, when the platform pays a bonus per order.' Choice C is a paraphrase of that line.

A.why: This was the economists' expectation, and the text rejects it. The top earners were 'not the longest-working couriers.'

B.why: Experience making couriers faster is only the reasoning behind the original expectation. The text never says the top earners were faster or more experienced.

D.why: Spreading bonuses across the day is Matos's suggested fix for the gap, not something that happens now. You took the proposed solution as the cause.

stem: According to the text, which of the following is NOT a feature of the fossil evidence Calderón's team examined?
stimulus: Researchers long assumed that the earliest flowering plants grew in dry, open habitats. However, a study led by paleobotanist Inés Calderón suggests otherwise. Her team examined 125-million-year-old fossil leaves recovered from a former lakebed in Portugal. The leaves are thin and broad, with dense networks of veins, traits found today mainly in plants of shaded, wet forest floors. The team also found pollen from the same species preserved beside the remains of aquatic insects.
choices: Leaves recovered from a former lakebed
Leaves with a thin and broad shape
Pollen preserved beside aquatic insects
Leaves typical of dry, open habitats
explanation: The phrase "dry, open habitats" does appear in the text, but in the first sentence. There it describes what researchers used to assume, not the fossils. The text says the leaves have traits typical of shaded, wet forest floors, the opposite of the old assumption. This is the only choice that doesn't describe the evidence, so it's the answer to a NOT question. Every word in it comes from the passage, but it answers a different question.

A.why: The text says the leaves were "recovered from a former lakebed in Portugal," so this is true. You found a statement you could support and picked it. The question asks for the one that is NOT a feature of the evidence.

B.why: The text says the leaves "are thin and broad," so this is true of the evidence. You likely matched it to the passage and stopped without noticing the NOT in the question.

C.why: The last sentence says the pollen was "preserved beside the remains of aquatic insects," so this is part of the evidence. Before you pick a choice in a NOT question, check whether the text supports it. If it does, that choice is wrong.

stem: According to the text, which of the following is NOT stated about slow-slip events?
stimulus: Slow-slip events, in which a fault moves over days or weeks rather than seconds, release built-up energy without producing strong shaking. Seismologist Kenji Arai found that along Japan's Nankai Trough, such events recur roughly every six months. Some observers have described them as a harmless way for faults to let off pressure. However, Arai cautions that slow slip may also add stress to neighboring locked sections of the fault, which could make a large earthquake there somewhat more likely.
choices: They unfold over a span of days or weeks.
They recur about twice a year at the Nankai Trough.
They may add stress to nearby locked fault sections.
They reliably prevent large earthquakes on the fault.
explanation: The text never says slow-slip events prevent large earthquakes. After "However," Arai warns that they may make a large earthquake somewhat more likely. The idea of "letting off pressure" belongs to "some observers," and the text sets that view up only to correct it. So this choice is the one that is not stated.

A.why: The first sentence says the fault moves "over days or weeks rather than seconds." This is stated, so it can't be the answer to a NOT question. You picked a true statement.

B.why: "Roughly every six months" means about twice a year, so this is stated in different words. If you rejected it because the wording doesn't match, convert the number before you decide. The text does support it.

C.why: This paraphrases Arai's caution that slow slip "may also add stress to neighboring locked sections." It is true, and it even keeps the hedge word "may," so it is not the exception.

stem: According to the text, which of the following is NOT true of the trial Nair's team conducted?
stimulus: Fiber is often credited for the heart benefits of whole oats. But nutrition scientist Priya Nair's team points to avenanthramides, compounds found in no other common cereal grain. In a twelve-week trial with 90 adults, participants who ate oat bran rich in these compounds showed lower markers of blood-vessel inflammation than those who ate oat bran with the compounds removed. It enrolled a total of 90 adults.
Its two groups ate equal amounts of fiber.
It compared oats with other cereal grains.
explanation: In the trial, both groups ate oat bran. One group's bran had avenanthramides and the other group's had them removed. No other grain was tested. The words "other common cereal grain" come from an earlier sentence, which explains what is special about the compounds. That sentence doesn't describe the trial, so this choice is not true of the trial.

A.why: The text calls it "a twelve-week trial," so this is true. You picked a statement the passage supports, but the question asks for the one that fails.

B.why: The text says the trial had "90 adults," so this is stated directly. In a NOT question, a choice you can point to in the text is a choice to eliminate.

C.why: The last sentence says "both groups consumed the same amount of fiber." This is true, and it is the reason the author credits the avenanthramides. It is not the exception.

stem: According to the text, how much larger was the drop in infection rates in wards with bedside dispensers than in wards with posters alone?
stimulus: Public health officials often credit hand-washing posters for declines in hospital infections. However, a review of twelve regional hospitals by epidemiologist Rana Okafor points elsewhere. In wards that also installed sanitizer dispensers beside every bed, rates fell by 19 percentage points over the same period. Okafor concludes that convenience, more than reminders, likely did most of the work.
choices: 12 percentage points
15 percentage points
19 percentage points
4 percentage points
explanation: The question asks about the gap between two groups. The text says rates fell by 19 percentage points in the dispenser wards and by 4 in the poster-only wards. 19 minus 4 is 15, so the dispenser wards' drop was 15 percentage points larger.

A.why: You took 12 from somewhere else in the passage. It is the number of hospitals Okafor reviewed, not a change in infection rates, so it answers a different question.

C.why: 19 is how much rates fell in the dispenser wards alone. The question asks how much larger that drop was than the poster-only drop, so you still need to subtract the 4.

D.why: 4 is how much rates fell in the poster-only wards. You answered about one group when the question asks for the difference between the two.

stem: According to the text, how much older was the water from the deep well than the water from the shallow well?

900 years
840 years
60 years

D.why: 60 years is the age of the shallow-well water. That is one side of the comparison, not the difference between the two ages.

stem: According to the text, how many more years before major repairs do engineers project for the fiber-reinforced deck than the original deck lasted?

33 years
75 years
20 years
